# Installing Gkeyll and postgkyl {.unnumbered}

You will install two things:

- **Gkeyll**, the simulation code. We build only its `core` and `moments`
  layers, which contain the multi-fluid solvers used in these lectures.
- **postgkyl**, the Python package for reading and plotting Gkeyll output,
  together with [marimo](https://marimo.io) for the lecture notebooks.

The instructions below are
[tested automatically every week](https://github.com/JunoRavin/reconnection-lectures/actions/workflows/install-test.yml),
with the latest version of Gkeyll, on macOS 15 (Apple silicon) and on Ubuntu
24.04 and 26.04 (with both Intel/AMD and ARM processors). They have not been
tested on Intel Macs.

On Windows, first install the
[Windows Subsystem for Linux](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install):
open PowerShell as an administrator, run `wsl --install`, and restart your
computer when it asks. Ubuntu then opens and asks you to choose a username and
password. Follow the Linux instructions below, running every command in that
Ubuntu terminal, not in PowerShell.

Expect the whole installation to take 15 to 40 minutes, depending on your
laptop (most of it is spent building Gkeyll's dependencies), and to use about
4 GB of disk space.

## 1. Prerequisites

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}

## macOS

Install Apple's command-line developer tools (compilers, `git`, `make`):

```bash
xcode-select --install
```

This opens a window asking to install the tools: click **Install** and wait
for it to finish before going on. If it instead prints a note that the
command line tools are already installed, you have them and can go on.

Next, check whether you have [Homebrew](https://brew.sh), a package manager
for macOS:

```bash
brew --version
```

If this prints `command not found`, install Homebrew by pasting the install
command from <https://brew.sh> into your terminal. On a Mac with Apple
silicon, Homebrew installs itself into a folder (`/opt/homebrew`) that your
terminal does not search for commands, so `brew` is still not found until you
add that folder to your path. The installer ends by listing these commands
under "Next steps"; run them yourself to be sure:

```bash
echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.zprofile
eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
```

The first line makes every new terminal find Homebrew, and the second does
the same for the terminal you have open. Check that `brew --version` now
works, then use Homebrew to install CMake:

```bash
brew install cmake
```

## Linux / WSL

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y build-essential gfortran cmake clang git curl rsync
```

`sudo` asks for your password (on WSL, the one you chose when you set up
Ubuntu). Nothing appears on the screen as you type it; press Enter when done.

:::

Finally, install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), which we use to set up
Python (it works the same way on both systems):

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

Open a new terminal window so that the `uv` command is found, and check that
`uv --version` prints a version number.

## 2. Build Gkeyll

Building Gkeyll involves two folders with similar names:

- **`~/gkeyll`** holds the source code, which you download below. Every build
  command runs inside this folder or its `install-deps` subfolder.
- **`~/gkylsoft`** is where the build installs the finished programs and
  libraries. You never run build commands there; you only look inside it to
  check that things were installed.

Each command block in this section starts by moving into the folder it needs,
so always run the whole block, including its first `cd` line. That way the
commands also work in a new terminal window, for example if you come back to
the installation the next day.

Download the source code into your home folder:

```bash
cd ~
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll.git
```

`--depth 1` downloads only the latest version of the code, not its whole
history, which makes the download about a third smaller. You can still update
it later (see [Updating Gkeyll](#updating-gkeyll)). If `git` reports that
`gkeyll` already exists, you downloaded it on an earlier attempt and can go
straight on to the next step.

### Build the dependencies

Gkeyll needs a few libraries (SuperLU, OpenMPI, LuaJIT, and on Linux,
OpenBLAS). The `mkdeps.sh` script in Gkeyll's `install-deps` folder downloads
and builds them into `~/gkylsoft`:

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}

## macOS

```bash
cd ~/gkeyll/install-deps
export MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=$(sw_vers -productVersion | cut -d. -f1-2)
./mkdeps.sh --build-superlu=yes --build-openmpi=yes --build-luajit=yes --prefix=$HOME/gkylsoft
```

The `export` line tells the LuaJIT build which version of macOS to target
(your own); without it, LuaJIT does not build.

## Linux / WSL

```bash
cd ~/gkeyll/install-deps
./mkdeps.sh --build-openblas=yes --build-superlu=yes --build-openmpi=yes --build-luajit=yes --prefix=$HOME/gkylsoft
```

:::

This is the longest step, typically 5 to 20 minutes depending on your laptop.
It prints thousands of lines, including many warnings, which are normal; it
is done when your prompt comes back.

The script keeps going even if one library fails to build, and a library's
name can appear in `~/gkylsoft` even when it failed. So before moving on,
check for one file that each library installs:

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}

## macOS

```bash
ls ~/gkylsoft/luajit/bin/luajit ~/gkylsoft/openmpi/bin/mpicc ~/gkylsoft/superlu/include/supermatrix.h
```

## Linux / WSL

```bash
ls ~/gkylsoft/luajit/bin/luajit ~/gkylsoft/openmpi/bin/mpicc ~/gkylsoft/superlu/include/supermatrix.h ~/gkylsoft/OpenBLAS/lib/libopenblas.a
```

:::

This prints each file's full path. If any line says `No such file or
directory` instead, that library did not build: scroll back through the
script's output to find the first error.

### Configure the build

Gkeyll's `configure` script records how Gkeyll should be built: which solvers
to include, which optional features to turn on, and where to find the
libraries you just built. It saves these settings in a file, `config.mak`,
which the compile step reads. It does not compile anything itself.

Run it from the `~/gkeyll` folder, not from `install-deps` (where the previous
step left your terminal) or from `~/gkylsoft`:

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}

## macOS

```bash
cd ~/gkeyll
./configure --prefix=$HOME/gkylsoft --use-mpi=yes --use-lua=yes --app=moments
```

## Linux / WSL

```bash
cd ~/gkeyll
./configure CC=clang --prefix=$HOME/gkylsoft --use-mpi=yes --use-lua=yes --app=moments
```

:::

The options mean:

- `--prefix=$HOME/gkylsoft`: install Gkeyll into `~/gkylsoft`, and look for
  the libraries from the previous step there.
- `--use-mpi=yes`: build with MPI, so that simulations can run in parallel.
- `--use-lua=yes`: build with Lua, the language Gkeyll input files are
  written in.
- `--app=moments`: build only the moments (multi-fluid) solvers these
  lectures use.
- `CC=clang` (Linux only): compile with Clang, which you installed in step 1,
  instead of the system's default compiler. On macOS the default compiler is
  already Clang.

The command finishes within a second and prints the settings it saved. Near
the top you should see

```
Building APP  moments
```

If you instead get an error saying `no such file or directory`, your terminal
is in a different folder; run the whole block again, starting with
`cd ~/gkeyll`.

`configure` does not check that the libraries are actually in `~/gkylsoft`.
A missing one only shows up as an error in the compile step, which is why you
checked with `ls` above. To change a setting, run `configure` again; it
replaces `config.mak`.

### Compile and install

Compile Gkeyll and install it into `~/gkylsoft`, again from the `~/gkeyll`
folder:

```bash
cd ~/gkeyll
make install -j 4
```

`-j 4` compiles four files at once. Each one needs up to about 1 GB of
memory, so this is fine on a laptop with 8 GB or more. If yours has more cores
and at least 16 GB of memory, a larger number is faster; to see how many cores
you have, run `sysctl -n hw.ncpu` on macOS or `nproc` on Linux.

Compiling takes a few minutes and prints a lot of output, including compiler
warnings, which you can ignore. If it stops with a line containing `Error`,
scroll up to the first line containing `error:` to see what went wrong. If
that line says a file cannot be found, a dependency probably did not build;
run the check at the end of the previous step again.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How this differs from Gkeyll's own instructions

Gkeyll's README builds with "machine files" such as
`./machines/mkdeps.macos.sh`. Those build every solver (including the much
larger kinetic and gyrokinetic ones) and download atomic data that only the
gyrokinetic solver uses. The commands above build the same dependencies but
only the solvers these lectures need.
:::

### Add Gkeyll to your path

Your terminal finds commands by searching a list of folders called your
*path*. The `gkeyll` and `mpirun` commands are in folders inside `~/gkylsoft`
that are not on it yet. This command adds them, by appending a line to the
file your terminal reads each time it starts (`~/.zshrc` on macOS, `~/.bashrc`
on Linux and WSL):

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}

## macOS

```bash
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/gkylsoft/gkeyll/bin:$HOME/gkylsoft/openmpi/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
```

## Linux / WSL

```bash
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/gkylsoft/gkeyll/bin:$HOME/gkylsoft/openmpi/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
```

:::

You only need to run it once. The change applies to terminals opened from now
on, so open a new terminal window and check that it worked:

```bash
gkeyll -v
```

You should see something like this, with your own changeset and date:

```
This is the Gkeyll code. See gkeyll.rtfd.io for details.
Type 'gkyl -h' for help.

Built with git changeset "69f896058907"
Built on "2026-11-18 12:56:48 CST"
Built without CUDA
```

If you get `command not found` instead, check that you opened a new terminal
window after running the `echo` command above.

## 3. Install postgkyl and marimo

Download these lectures, which include the notebooks and simulation input
files, into `~/reconnection-lectures`, and create a Python environment (a
folder named `.venv`) inside it:

```bash
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/JunoRavin/reconnection-lectures.git
cd ~/reconnection-lectures
uv venv --python 3.12 --managed-python
```

Download postgkyl into `~/postgkyl` and install it, together with marimo,
into that environment. `uv pip install` installs into the `.venv` folder of
the folder you are in, which is why this block starts in
`~/reconnection-lectures`. Installing postgkyl compiles a small extension
that connects it to Gkeyll's data format, so this step takes a minute or so:

```bash
cd ~/reconnection-lectures
git clone https://github.com/gkeyllorg/postgkyl.git ~/postgkyl
uv pip install ~/postgkyl marimo
```

To use postgkyl and marimo, activate the environment. Do this whenever you
open a new terminal to work on the lectures; the command works from any
folder:

```bash
source ~/reconnection-lectures/.venv/bin/activate
```

While the environment is active, your prompt starts with
`(reconnection-lectures)`.

## 4. Check your installation

Gkeyll comes with a small version of the GEM reconnection problem that the
lectures study. Run it in a scratch folder (this takes well under a minute):

```bash
mkdir -p ~/gkeyll-check && cd ~/gkeyll-check
cp ~/gkeyll/moments/luareg/rt_10m_gem.lua .
gkeyll rt_10m_gem.lua
```

When it finishes, the folder contains `.gkyl` output files. Activate the
lecture environment and load the final electromagnetic field with postgkyl:

```bash
cd ~/gkeyll-check
source ~/reconnection-lectures/.venv/bin/activate
python -c "import postgkyl as pg; print(pg.load('rt_10m_gem-field_1.gkyl').get_values().shape)"
```

This should print (the first time, after a message about Matplotlib building
its font cache)

```
(128, 64, 8)
```

that is, the field on the 128 × 64 grid of this test problem, with eight
components: the three components each of the electric and magnetic fields, and
two potentials Gkeyll uses to keep the divergence constraints satisfied.

If you see this, everything is installed and you are ready to
[run the simulations](running.qmd).

## Updating Gkeyll

These instructions install the latest version of Gkeyll, which changes
often. If you are asked to update it, for example to pick up a fix, run:

```bash
cd ~/gkeyll
git pull
make install -j 4
```

This downloads the changes and recompiles only the files they affect. You do
not need to build the dependencies or run `configure` again: your settings are
kept in `config.mak`, which `git pull` leaves alone.
